cli.help.group.login:
Sign in to a harness (`login` is a group of commands, not an interactive program; the web page's Settings → Sign-in does the same):
  1. {command} workspace catalog                      see the node id (nodes[].id) and the existing profiles
  2. {command} profile create-managed --agent codex --node-id <node id> --label "My Codex"
                                                  create a profile with its own sign-in (this machine's existing sign-in is untouched)
  3. {command} login start <profile id>                start signing in; the answer has the sign-in flow's id
  4. {command} login show <flow id>                    get the authorization address (url, userCode) and open it in a browser on any machine
  5. {command} login input <flow id>                   when the authorization page gives a code, hand it over (prompted, not echoed)
  6. {command} login show <flow id>                    done when status becomes complete; cancel with {command} login cancel <flow id>
Claude with an API key: {command} profile create --agent claude --auth-mode apiKey --node-id <node id> --label "My key" --api-key (prompts for the key, not echoed).
cli.help.group.session:
Common: {command} session create … → {command} session send <id> "message" → {command} session show <id>;
archive: {command} session update <id> --archived; the AI's tool approvals and questions are answered only on the web page ({command} open).

cli.local.autostart.help:
on: on Linux, creates and enables a systemd user unit (~/.config/systemd/user/{command}.service); on macOS, writes a LaunchAgent (~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.{command}.{command}.plist) that launchd starts after you log in; on Windows, writes a Run entry for the current user ({product} under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) that {product}'s Windows supervisor starts after you sign in. After that, {command} start / stop go through systemd / launchd / that supervisor.
off: disables and removes it (a running {product} is not affected; it no longer starts at the next boot / login).
Without an argument: shows the current state.
On macOS, keep it on: launchd starts it in your login session, the only way Claude's keychain sign-in can be read.

cli.local.start.help:
With autostart on ({command} autostart on), systemd (Linux) or launchd (macOS) starts it; otherwise it starts as a background process and writes its output to logs/{command}.log in the data directory.
On macOS, turn autostart on first: launchd starts it in your login session, the only way Claude's keychain sign-in can be read.
No port needed: it is derived from the account's uid, and if that one is taken a free one is found and remembered. The data directory follows the system's convention; --data-dir or DAISY_DATA changes it.

Options:
  --port <port>     the local face's port, 1024–65535 (an error if it is taken, never silently changed)
  --foreground      run in the foreground in this terminal (for debugging, or for another service manager)
cli.local.start.launchdAdvice: Tip: on macOS, hand it to launchd with {command} autostart on — launchd starts {product} in your login session, the only way Claude's keychain sign-in can be read (a background process started from a restricted terminal can't read it); after that, {command} stop and {command} start go through launchd

Autostart stays as it is: it starts again at the next boot (to turn that off: {command} autostart off).

cli.local.update.help:
Without options: the version installed on disk, the version running, a new version found, the auto-update switch, and how the last update went.
Switching versions needs a restart, and a restart interrupts a running turn (never replayed), so by default it waits until fully idle.
Before switching, it backs up the database (backups/ in the data directory) and keeps the current version's package to fall back on (update/packages/); if the new version isn't running normally within 120 seconds, it rolls back by itself.
The commands are the same on Linux, macOS and Windows, and work while {product} is not running too (the next start backs up the database first, then tries the new version).

Options:
  --check            check the update source once now, without installing (there is no default source: --source first)
  --apply            once idle, switch to the newest version in the source (even with auto-update off); after a manual npm install -g of a new version, switch to that once idle
  --from <tgz>       with --apply: switch to this package on this machine
  --allow-downgrade  with --apply: allow switching to an older version
  --rollback         switch back to the previous version (the package kept in the data directory)
  --source <source>  set the update source (needs the PIN): a directory of .tgz files or one .tgz (absolute path), npm:{package}@latest (once this scope is registered and the package published), off; none removes it
  --now              restart right away: first lists the sessions it would interrupt, goes ahead once you confirm
  --cancel           withdraw a restart / update request not yet carried out

The restart calls can also be used directly: {command} restart status|request|cancel.
cli.local.update.howTo: To update: {command} update --apply (the newest in the source) or {command} update --apply --from <tgz>; or npm install -g <new version>, and {product} switches to it by itself once idle.

cli.local.watch.help:
One event per line on standard output (CloudEvents 1.0 JSON, see docs/contracts/events.md); status notes go to standard error.
Without --after and without a cursor file, it first takes a snapshot (every card not yet settled), then reads on from the snapshot's sequence number; after that it long-polls and prints new events as they arrive.
When {product} restarts or can't be reached for a while, it waits for it and reads on from the same sequence number; when that number can't be continued (old events cleared, data rebuilt), it takes a new snapshot.

Options:
  --after <seq>          start reading after this sequence number (no snapshot)
  --cursor-file <file>   keep the sequence number read in this file (saved after each page) and read on from it next time; stopping mid-page reads the same page again, so de-duplicate by the event's id
  --wait <seconds>       the longest each wait lasts (1–{max}, default {max})
  --max <count>          exit after printing this many events (for scripts)

Just one page: {command} events list --after <seq>; a snapshot: {command} events snapshot.
cli.local.watch.summary: Follow the event outlet: AI approval requests, AI questions and calls waiting for approval, as they appear and are settled
cli.logHint: {file} (under systemd: journalctl --user -u {command}*; under launchd it writes this file too)
cli.options.none: This command has no options (more in {command} {cmd} --help)
cli.pin.noGrant: {product} did not hand out a PIN grant
cli.pin.noGrantFix: Try once more; if it still fails, {command} doctor
cli.pinNotSet: ⚠ No PIN is set yet: run {command} pin set first, or no AI will start working
cli.process.exitedFix: deal with the cause above; the full log is in {log}
cli.process.hung: process {pid} holds this data directory ({dir}) but does not answer
cli.process.hungFix: it may be stuck: {command} stop (kill {pid} if needed), then {command} start; log {log}
cli.process.launchdStartFix: someone must be logged in to this Mac's desktop (only then does launchd's {domain} domain exist): log in, then {command} start; see launchctl print {target}; or {command} autostart off, then {command} start (runs as a background process; started from a restricted terminal it cannot read the keychain)
cli.process.launchdStopFix: see launchctl print {target}; or launchctl kill SIGTERM {target}
cli.process.noPermissionFix: run {command} stop as the same system account that runs {product}
cli.process.noServerFix: the installation is incomplete: reinstall (npm install -g <the {command} tgz package>)
cli.process.notListening: waited {seconds, plural, one {# second} other {# seconds}} and {product} is not listening yet{tail}
cli.process.notListeningFix: see the log {log} (under systemd: journalctl --user -u {command}*); once fixed, {command} stop, then {command} start
cli.process.notOurs: process {pid} in the runtime file does not look like {product} (it does not answer and is not {product}'s program), so it was left alone
cli.process.notOursFix: check and handle it yourself: ps -p {pid}; if it really is not {product}, just delete {dir}/runtime.json
cli.process.portManaged: with autostart on, the port is set by {by}; --port cannot be used
cli.process.portManagedFix: first {command} autostart off, then start with --port; or start without --port (the port is derived from the uid and remembered)
cli.process.stillThere: waited {seconds, plural, one {# second} other {# seconds}} and process {pid} has not exited
cli.process.stillThereFix: it may still be finishing up: wait a little and look with {command} status; to force it: {kill} (a running turn is cut off, marked interrupted at the next start and never replayed)
cli.process.systemdStartFix: see journalctl --user -u {unit}; or {command} autostart off, then {command} start (runs as a background process)
cli.routes.notDefined: This version of the command line has no route {id}
cli.routes.notDefinedFix: The command line and {product} must be the same version: after reinstalling, {command} stop, {command} start
cli.status.autoUpdate.available: new version {target} is available (auto-update is off: {command} update --apply switches to it)
cli.status.autoUpdate.no-source: no update source set ({command} update --source <dir | .tgz | npm:@daisy-ai/daisy@latest>, or updateSource in runner.json)
cli.status.autostart.launchdDisabled: the plist is there but disabled (launchd login item {unit}; starts after you log in)
cli.status.autostart.launchdOn: on (launchd login item {unit}; starts after you log in)
cli.status.autostart.noLinger: ; linger is off, so it starts only after you log in
cli.status.autostart.systemdDisabled: the unit is there but not enabled (systemd user unit {unit}{linger})
cli.status.autostart.windows: on (the current user's Run entry {unit}; starts after you sign in to Windows)
cli.status.externalNotListening: on, but not listening (see the log)
cli.status.externalOff: off (to open it from other machines: {command} access external on, needs the PIN)
cli.status.fingerprint: self-signed certificate SHA-256: {fingerprint} (check the certificate in the browser; go on only if the fingerprints match)
cli.status.managed.windows: the supervisor of the Windows Run entry {unit} (log {log})
cli.status.notAnswering: {product}'s process {pid} is there but does not answer (starting, or stuck)
cli.status.passcodeOn: in effect ({command} open prints a link with a one-time passcode)
cli.status.pin.locked: set; locked after wrong tries until {until}
cli.status.pin.unavailable: this version has no PIN yet
cli.status.portSource.moved: the remembered port was taken; another one for this run
cli.status.portSource.remembered: chosen at the first start and remembered
cli.status.problemHint: everything else works; restart after fixing it ({command} stop && {command} start); details: {command} doctor
cli.status.relay.certAcme: a certificate from a certificate authority
cli.status.relay.certSelf: a self-signed certificate: only other Daisies can use it through the relay
cli.status.relay.off: none chosen (to be called from other networks: {command} relay set <relay address>, needs the PIN)
cli.status.staleNote: It did not exit cleanly last time (process {pid} is gone); {command} start starts afresh
cli.status.stuckHint: See the log: {log}; if it is stuck, {command} stop, then {command} start
cli.status.update.autoNoSource: auto-update: no update source set ({command} update --source <dir | .tgz | npm:@daisy-ai/daisy@latest>, or updateSource in runner.json)
cli.status.update.foreground: running in the foreground: an installed new version does not switch in by itself (see {command} update)
cli.status.update.found: new version {target} was found and switches in when idle (waiting for: {waiting})
cli.status.update.installed: new version {target} is installed and switches in when idle (waiting for: {waiting})
cli.status.update.nothing: no update to do ({command} update for details)
cli.status.update.restartIdle: a restart request (when idle) is pending
cli.table.badJsonFix: check the quotes and brackets; in a shell, put the whole JSON in single quotes
cli.table.binary: this is binary content and cannot be printed to the terminal
cli.table.binaryFix: add --output <file> to save it, or redirect it to a file with >
cli.table.card.badFix: ask the other person to export the card again and send it complete, then import it
cli.table.card.expectGiven: --expect-id given: if the number does not match, it is not added to your contacts.
cli.table.card.expectHint: Once checked, you can import with --expect-id {prefix}: if the number does not match, it is not added to your contacts.
cli.table.card.name: Card: {name}
cli.table.card.verify: First check this number with the other person, in person or by phone (at least the first {n} characters): a card only proves "the content comes from whoever holds this key", not whose key it is.
cli.table.extraArgsFix: see {command} {cmd} --help for usage; put text with spaces in quotes
cli.table.mismatchFix: run the command again and type the same value twice
cli.table.noBody: this command takes no request body: --json cannot be used
cli.table.notBoolean: {label} is true or false; "{raw}" is not
cli.table.own.answer: The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
cli.table.own.idempotencyKey: --idempotency-key <key>  the idempotency key (generated by default); resending with the same key after a disconnect never runs it twice
cli.table.own.jsonBody: --json <body>            the whole request body (JSON; @file reads a file, - standard input)
cli.table.own.jsonObject: --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
cli.table.own.output: --output <file>          save the download to a file (default: standard output)
cli.table.own.title: Common options:
cli.table.pair.howCode: On the other device, open the outside face's web page, choose "Connect this device with a pairing code" on the login page and type in the code.
cli.table.pair.howLink: Open this link in the browser of the other device (a phone, say), or open the outside face's web page, choose "Connect this device with a pairing code" on the login page and enter the code.
cli.table.pair.noLink: (no link: type the pairing code on the device)
cli.table.pair.valid: Valid for {mins, plural, one {# minute} other {# minutes}}, once. A paired device connects as you: when you no longer need it, {command} device revoke <id>.
cli.table.rawBody: this command takes the whole request body with --json
cli.table.readFileFix: check the path and the permissions
cli.table.resendHint: ; once connected, resend with --idempotency-key {key}: it will not run twice
cli.table.saved: saved to {path} ({bytes, plural, one {# byte} other {# bytes}})
cli.table.secretOnLine: {name} is a credential and cannot be written on the command line (it would stay in the shell history and the process list)
cli.table.secretOnLineFix: write just {flag} (no value) and the command asks for it; or give it on standard input (one per line)
cli.table.token.how: A third-party A2A client sends it the standard way: Authorization: Bearer <the line below>
cli.table.token.issued: Issued a token: for {who}, id {id}, expires {expires}.
cli.watch.cursorBad: The cursor file {file} does not hold a sequence number: “{text}”
cli.watch.cursorBadFix: Delete it (reading starts again from a snapshot), or write the last sequence number into it
cli.watch.cursorUnreadableFix: Use a path that can be read and written, or drop --cursor-file
cli.watch.down: {product} can't be reached ({why}): waiting for it to come back, then reading on from sequence {cursor}
cli.watch.downSnapshot: {product} can't be reached ({why}): waiting for it to come back, then starting from a snapshot
cli.watch.reconnected: Reconnected to {product}; reading on from sequence {cursor}
cli.watch.reset: Sequence {cursor} can't be continued (old events were cleared, or {product}'s data was rebuilt): taking a new snapshot
cli.watch.snapshot: Snapshot: {n} card(s) not yet settled; reading on from sequence {cursor} (Ctrl-C to stop)
